By the time Mara and Tovin reached the survey stone, the red weather had stopped.

Someone upriver had called the dawn a wound, and all morning light had been seeping from the roofs and collecting in the ditches. Now it was drying into flakes of gold. The wind lifted them in small, bright scabs and carried them east.

The stone stood where the road should have been.

Instead, two roads began there. One climbed toward the mountain through juniper and exposed limestone. The other went down into a valley neither of them could quite see. Whenever Mara tried to look directly at it, she found herself reading the inscription again.

Tovin leaned close.

“‘The mountain overlooks—’”

Something opened beneath his left boot.

Not a hole exactly. The grass still grew around it, and a beetle continued along the rim, but within it there was no depth, no color, and no convincing distance. Far away, a bell rang once and seemed embarrassed.

“Finish,” said Mara.

“‘—the valley.’”

The opening stopped growing. It remained beside the road, about the size of a supper plate. Tovin moved his boot. A fine grey dust fell from the sole and vanished before reaching the ground.

Mara read the sentence herself.

“The mountain overlooks the valley.”

Above them, stone shifted against stone. Pines shivered. The mountain rose by perhaps the height of a tower, and from its new elevation the valley sprang suddenly into view: river, bridge, mill, orchards, forty or fifty slate roofs arranged along a green fold of land.

The climbing road widened.

“There,” said Tovin. “A surveyor’s sentence. It has a view of the valley. We take the ridge.”

“It might fail to notice the valley.”

The roofs lost their edges.

Not all at once. First Mara could no longer tell where the mill ended and its reflection began. Then the river stopped glittering. The bridge remained, but it crossed from one vagueness to another.

The lower road narrowed.

Tovin looked at her with dislike. “Why would you say that?”

“Because it might.”

“It doesn’t.”

The mountain settled. The river flashed. A white cloth appeared on a line beside one of the houses, distinct enough that they could see it was patched at one corner.

“It commands a prospect,” Tovin said. “That is what overlooks means on a map.”

“It means both.”

“Not here.”

“Especially here.”

The road beneath them gave a small, thoughtful shudder. A third path considered appearing between the other two, then thought better of it.

Tovin pointed toward the summit. “If it overlooks the valley, the ridge road must be visible from there. Someone will see us. We’ll know where we are.”

“If it overlooks the valley,” Mara said, “we may walk the whole ridge without finding so much as a stream.”

The mountain gave a deep mineral sigh. Its upper ridge leaned almost imperceptibly away.

This time the valley did not blur. It became easy to miss.

Mara could see all of it if she kept her eyes moving: an orchard while glancing at the river, a church tower behind Tovin’s shoulder, three black cows in the corner of her vision when she looked up at the clouds. But whenever she tried to assemble the whole valley, her attention slid politely elsewhere.

Something else was appearing down there.

Between the orchard and the river stood a house with too many chimneys. Behind the mill, a flight of steps descended into the sky. A small moon, no bigger than a barrel lid, was caught in the branches of an oak. It had a face, though perhaps that was only a trick of the craters.

Tovin saw it too.

“That wasn’t there before.”

“The mountain hadn’t failed to notice it before.”

“Mountains don’t notice things.”

“You were happy enough to give this one a view.”

“A view is geography.”

“A view is an appetite with good manners.”

The mountain rose again at *geography*, then sank at *appetite*. Somewhere on its slopes an avalanche started, reconsidered, and came back uphill as a white flock of birds.

Tovin took off his pack and sat on it. “I liked this country better when people were afraid of adjectives.”

Mara went to the edge of the lower road.

From there she could see a garden that had not been visible from the stone. Beans climbed the skeleton of an enormous fish. A woman in a blue dress was hanging spoons from an apple tree. She looked up at Mara, not with surprise but with the mild irritation of someone whose privacy had been carelessly included in a sentence.

Behind her, half concealed by a lilac, stood a red door.

Mara knew the door. She had last seen it forty years ago, from the wrong side, while her mother was telling someone that Mara had probably just wandered off and would come back when she was hungry.

She had come back. The door had not.

Tovin joined her. “No.”

“You don’t know what I’m going to say.”

“You’re going to say we should go down.”

“I wasn’t.”

“Good.”

“I was going to say you could stay here.”

Below them, the woman in blue hung the last spoon. All the spoons began turning, though there was no wind in the valley. Their bowls reflected different weather: snow, a hard little sun, the green light before hail, a darkness full of wings.

Tovin rubbed his face. “If the mountain looks down on the valley, then the valley stays. Your door stays. We can find it sensibly.”

At *stays*, the red door acquired a wall. Then a whole house. Then neat rows of cabbages, a woodshed, a road leading to the bridge. The little moon vanished from the oak.

Mara’s hand tightened around the strap of her pack.

“And if it doesn’t?” she asked.

Tovin was silent.

The mountain’s shadow moved over them. It was cool and smelled faintly of wet iron. Far below, in the unsteady space between one interpretation and the other, the red door opened by itself.

There was no room beyond it. Only a narrow beach, at night, with two sets of footprints going into the sea and none coming out. Something on the sand was writing with a piece of driftwood.

Mara stepped onto the lower road.

Tovin caught her sleeve. “Wait. If we both read it differently—”

The sentence split the air with a sound like ice cracking on a lake.

For an instant the mountain stood above a bright, comprehensible valley. For an instant there was no valley at all, only an omission full of weather. Then both were there together, laid one over the other: the mill turning and motionless, the river silver and unseen, the red door opening onto a beach and onto a kitchen where a kettle had just begun to boil.

Tovin let go of her sleeve.

“Well,” he said, and stopped.

A small gap appeared in his shadow.

They walked around it. Behind them, the survey stone began, very slowly, to turn its inscription toward the sea.

1. Every tick has exactly one echo, occurring one minute earlier and half as loud.
2. The sole listener hears every tick. One minute after hearing one, it repeats that tick twice as loud. There are no other sources of ticks.
3. At noon there is a tick of loudness 1.

At 11:59 there must be a tick of loudness ½: noon’s echo. Having heard it, the listener must repeat it at noon, at loudness 1.

The cleanest reading makes this repetition the same event as the tick given at noon.

Removing one would remove the echo required from the minute before it, then the repetition required in the minute after it, until the whole sequence came loose.

The past never begins in silence. It merely becomes softer than any chosen positive loudness while continuing to contain ticks, each one heard, each one sufficient to require the entire louder future. The future likewise never becomes too loud for a final tick; there is always another hearing, another repetition.

The listener therefore cannot have a quietest audible sound or a loudest bearable one. Its hearing is not a finite interval. It is less like an ear than like the agreement by which one minute recognizes the next.
